extracted.intended_audience: general readers; fans and researchers of adult animation and Adult Swim programming
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article documenting the TV series Squidbillies: its genre, premise, production, cast, episodes, and distribution. Useful as a reference for readers researching the show's style, history, and credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed genres: Adult animation; Animated sitcom; Satire; Surreal humour; Black comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording in infobox: 'Genre: Adult animation, Animated sitcom, Satire, Surreal humour, Black comedy.' Use these genre labels when classifying the series' comedic register and intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise and Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Follows the Cuylers, an impoverished family of anthropomorphic hillbilly 'mud squids' living in the Georgia Blue Ridge Mountains; central characters include Early (lazy, ornery alcoholic and frequent criminal), Rusty (good-natured son), Granny (very old, many health problems), Lil (hairdresser, sex worker, meth cook), Sheriff (friendly, incompetent), and Dan Halen (evil exploitative robber baron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The series' comedy and plots revolve around the exploits of these characters and their interactions with the local populace, often leading to extreme outcomes (destruction, mutilation, death). Use character archetypes and premise to evaluate storylines and tonal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical targets / Themes
rubrics_metrics.description: The show often satirizes the history and culture of the American South, including the Lost Cause, slavery, religious fundamentalism, segregation, political conservatism, bigotry, racism, and poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit list from article: these are recurring thematic targets. The New York Times phrasing notes the show 'takes "backwoods stereotypes" and turns them into "a cudgel with which to pound maniacally on all manner of topical subjects."' Use presence and handling of these themes to assess the show's satirical intent and topicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animation style and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Described as 'Beavis and Butt-Head style'; based on Adobe Flash / Macromedia Shockwave Flash; characters deliberately drawn crudely 'by design'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production details: Radical Axis animated until 2012; Awesome Inc from season 7 onward. Main software allowed easier HD rendering. The article states 'The series' animation ... is based on Adobe Flash and takes a week to complete' and 'An average episode took about 700 working hours to complete.' Use these technical and stylistic facts to evaluate visual aesthetics, production constraints, and fidelity to intended crude style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and development process
rubrics_metrics.description: Created by Jim Fortier and Dave Willis; written primarily and entirely by them (occasionally aided by other writers); pilot and early development involved many rewrites (over 35 scripts written during development).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes delays due to lack of ideas, multiple rewrites, character name changes, and shifting of concepts among related Adult Swim projects. Use authorship, rewrite volume, and development anecdotes to assess authors' creative control and script evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production process and schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Production took place exclusively in Atlanta with between five and seven animators; no storyboards or particular animations were produced; production times could take up to eight weeks, later seasons often completed within a few weeks to a month before revisiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these production workflow details (in-house animation, small team, limited storyboarding) to understand turnaround, resource allocation, and how process shapes final episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backgrounds and visual art style
rubrics_metrics.description: Backgrounds and colors created by Ben Prisk at Primal Screen; based on folk art; characterized by lack of right angles and confusing perspectives; created in acrylic, revisited with gouache and spray paint, composed in Adobe Photoshop; each wallpaper took around 12–15 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specifics justify the show's distinctive background aesthetics; evaluate episodes for alignment with the intended folk-art, distorted-perspective look described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode format and running time
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical running time: 11 minutes (one episode—episode 60—ran 22 minutes). Series run: 13 seasons, 132 episodes (original release October 16, 2005 – December 12, 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episode length and season/episode counts when assessing pacing, narrative density, and series longevity. Note occasional deviations from standard runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice casting and personnel changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice cast includes Stuart Daniel Baker (2005–2019) as Early Cuyler, Daniel McDevitt as Rusty, Dana Snyder as Granny, Patricia French as Aunt Lil, and others. Stuart Baker was fired August 16, 2020, for controversial comments and later replaced by Tracy Morgan for season 13.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting continuity, controversies, and replacement choices (public responses, auditions) are relevant when evaluating character portrayal consistency and public-relations impacts on the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest appearances and musical contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous guest voice actors and musical guest performances across episodes (e.g., Fred Armisen, Patton Oswalt, Coolio, Drive-By Truckers, Widespread Panic, Jason Isbell, many others). Artists also performed or recorded versions of the theme song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guest and musical contributions often shape individual episode tone and can signal cultural reach; evaluate episodes for the integration and effect of guest performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home media, soundtrack, and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Series released on various DVD volumes with extras (deleted scenes, commentaries, behind-the-scenes), a free 35-track soundtrack released January 2012, a vinyl album in July 2019, and availability on HBO Max since September 1, 2020 (seasons 1–12 removed in 2023 pending return).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution history and extras inform accessibility, archival quality, and commercial footprint. Use release details when discussing fan access and supplemental materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and content (adult/explicit elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Series content includes destruction, mutilation, death, drug use (meth cooking), sex work, alcoholism, and extreme black comedy elements (e.g., Lil often found unconscious in a pool of her own vomit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article foregrounds mature and potentially offensive content; cite these content elements when assessing suitability for audiences, trigger warnings, and the show's adherence to black-comedy conventions.
